Openshaw, a brave soldier, but with the Southern sympathies,
found himself after the war in the power of this terrible
organisation. They sent him their usual warning. He burned their
papers, but they still had their hold upon him. Then he fled to
England. But he was afraid that they would follow him and take
their revenge. And at last they did. He hid his fear from me,
but I can read it in the lines of his face. That is why the
papers were so important. The society could not afford that
they should fall into the hands of the American Government. That
is why they pursued him across the ocean. That is why they
destroyed him and his son."

"But the sundial?"

"Why, my dear Watson, what is a sundial without a shadow?"

"That is our society," said Holmes, replacing the volume upon the
shelf.  "These fellows are evidently trying to recover some
papers which Colonel Openshaw took with him when he fled from
America. They are the same men who pursued him across the ocean,
and who, in spite of his precautions, have hunted him down. If
young Openshaw had come to us a few hours ago, the result might
have been different, but now--" He paused.

"You see it all now?" Holmes asked, turning to me.  "Colonel
Openshaw had evidently incurred the vengeance of this formidable
society, and had fled from them to England.  He had carried some
secret with him, some document or some papers which would be of
great use to the society. They pursued him, and he burned the
bulk of their papers in the attempt to safeguard them. They sent
their warning in the form of the familiar orange pips.  He
ignored it, and so was killed.  His brother disregarded their
warning, also, and he likewise met his death."

"That," said Holmes, putting his finger upon the passage, "is our
case exactly. The Klan has long been broken up, but there are
still some of the old organization remaining. They are fewer in
number, they are more scattered, they are less audacious in their
methods, but their traditions still remain. Colonel Openshaw,
while in Florida, had evidently incurred their enmity. He fled to
England, but they hunted him down. They sent a warning--those
pips--before they struck him down. They watched him, and they
followed him to his death, but they could not do it without
sending the warning. His brother inherited the quarrel, and they
struck him down also. Now it is the young man's turn, and it would
have been done had not we interfered."

"You see it all now?" Holmes asked, turning to me.  "Colonel
Openshaw played a dangerous game in opposing the Ku Klux Klan.  He
fled to England, but they tracked him down.  The papers he
destroyed were, no doubt, damaging to the society, and they mean
to recover them at all costs."

"You will observe," said Holmes, laying down the volume, "that
the sudden breaking up of the society was coincident with the
disappearance of Openshaw from America with their papers. It may
well have been cause and effect. It is no wonder that he and his
family have some of the more implacable spirits upon their track.
You can understand that this register and diary may implicate
some of the first men in the South, and that there may be many
who will not sleep easy at night until it is recovered."

"Then the page we have seen--"

"'A terrible tragedy occurred yesterday afternoon, about three
o'clock, close to Waterloo Bridge. Mr. John Openshaw, the young
gentleman who inherits the Openshaw estates near Horsham, was
found dead near the edge of the Victoria Embankment. From the
position of the body and the marks upon his neck it is obvious
that he had been strangled. There seems to be no clue as to the
murderers, and the police are completely at a loss. The deceased
gentleman was last seen leaving his hotel about noon, and it is
supposed that he was waylaid as he returned.'

"That's the end of it," I remarked with a sigh, "and a most
horrible end."

"You will observe," said Holmes, "that the case is complete.
They have acted more swiftly than I could have conceived possible.
They must have had a boat at hand, or it would have been too late
to take advantage of this most unfortunate accident."

"‘A shocking tragedy occurred yesterday afternoon close to
Waterloo Bridge. A young gentleman, Mr. John Openshaw, well known
in the Horsham district, was found dead upon the pavement with a
single gunshot wound in the head. No papers or valuables were
missing, and no weapon was discovered. The police have come to
the conclusion that the unfortunate victim must have been shot
from behind and that the murderer then escaped by means of the
crowded thoroughfare.' That is the official account, Holmes."

"'A shocking murder was committed last night near Waterloo
Bridge. Mr. John Openshaw, the young heir to the Openshaw
estate, was found dead near the edge of the water, his skull
fractured in several places. There were no signs of robbery, and
no clue as to the murderer. It is thought that the tragic event
is not unconnected with the deaths of his father and uncle, which
were also investigated by the police, but resulted in no
apprehension. It is understood that the young man had had
several warnings that his life was in danger, but the police do
not regard this as a serious matter.'"

"‘A shocking murder was committed last night near Waterloo
Bridge. Mr. John Openshaw, the young landed proprietor of
Horsham, was found dead near the edge of the Victoria Embankment
with his skull fractured. There would appear to have been no
robbery, as his watch and money were untouched. No trace has
been found of the murderer, but it is believed that the police
have a clue.'"

"'A terrible tragedy occurred last night, about eleven o'clock,
close to Waterloo Bridge. Mr. John Openshaw, the young
gentleman who has recently come into a large fortune, was found
lying on the pavement at the foot of the steps which lead down
from the bridge to the Embankment. His skull was fractured, and
he was quite dead. There would appear to have been no robbery,
since his watch and money were still in his possession, and there
is no indication of any struggle. It is assumed that Mr.
Openshaw had fallen from the bridge, as there is some evidence
of his having been on it about that hour.' This is what it
says."

I refolded the paper and laid it upon the table. It was some
minutes before Holmes could speak. The excitement and the
disappointment of the morning had left their mark upon his
usually keen and alert face.

"Between nine and ten last night Police-Constable Cook, of the H
Division, on duty near Waterloo Bridge, heard a cry for help and
a splash in the water. The night, however, was extremely dark and
stormy, so that, in spite of the help of several passers-by, it
was quite impossible to effect a rescue. The alarm, however, was
given, and, by the aid of the water-police, the body was
eventually recovered. It proved to be that of a young gentleman
whose name, as it appears from an envelope which was found in his
pocket, was John Openshaw, and whose residence is near Horsham.
It is conjectured that he may have been hurrying down to catch
the last train from Waterloo Station, and that in his haste and
the extreme darkness he missed his path and walked over the edge
of one of the small landing-places for river steamboats. The body
exhibited no traces of violence, and there can be no doubt that
the deceased had been the victim of an unfortunate accident,
which should have the effect of calling the attention of the
authorities to the condition of the riverside landing-stages."

We sat in silence for some minutes, Holmes more depressed and
shaken than I had ever seen him.

"They shall not escape me, Watson! They shall not escape. I have
a scent, I have a scent, I tell you! They shall not escape. I
will follow them to the ends of the earth!"  He stopped suddenly
and his face cleared.  "Come, Watson, come!  The game is afoot.
The papers are of more importance than ever now. We must find
them."

"We must act quickly, Watson," he said at last. "The first thing
is to find this sailing vessel. She is probably in the Thames,
and we must trace her. With that object I shall go down to the
docks and make inquiries among the shipping agents. It is a
singular case, and one which will tax all our energies. I have
already grasped one or two points which seem to indicate the
direction in which we should move."

"The game is afoot," he cried at last, his voice ringing through
the room. "We shall hunt them down, Watson! We shall hunt them
down!"  He seized his hat and rushed from the flat, leaving me to
wonder at the grim determination which shone in his eyes. I had
little doubt that the pursuit would be a hot one, and I felt a
certain thrill of excitement in the prospect of the chase.

"They shall not escape me, Watson! They shall not escape. I shall
have them yet!" His voice vibrated with a fierce energy as he
spoke.  "We must act quickly, and methodically." He paused, his
eyes shining with a cold light. "Our first step is to visit Mr.
James Calhoun, I believe.  He is a man I have cause to remember, and who may know more about this matter than he cares to admit."


"They were cunning, these devils," he said at last, resuming his
seat. "I shall never forgive myself for not having taken his
case more seriously at the time. Had he gone straight to his
house after leaving us, all would have been well. But he must
needs return to his lodgings to fetch his umbrella and coat. That
was his ruin. They were waiting for him. He was probably
followed from here."

"They must be cunning devils," he exclaimed at last. "How could
they have decoyed him down there? The Embankment is not on the
direct line to the station. The bridge, no doubt, was too
crowded, even on such a night, for their purpose. Well, Watson,
we shall see who will win in the long run. I am going out now!"

"To the police?"

"No; I shall be my own police. When I have spun the web they may
take the flies, but not before."

"I mean that we shall use their own methods against them.
Remember that curious stain upon the blue paper? It was a sort of
clay and chalk mixture. I have just been testing it, and it
appears to be the very distinctive earth of the Horsham district.
That is enough to show that the villain lives near Horsham. But
the question was, which one of those four suspects was the true
culprit? Well, consider. The pips were sent to each of the
victims in a unique manner, showing how the culprit was
constantly near the victim, thus eliminating James Calhoun who
lived in America. That narrowed the selection to three brothers,
John, Joseph, and Elias Openshaw. But then, consider that the
same letter was sent to each victim, yet it was sent from
different locations. This showed me that the culprit must have
been someone who could easily travel between the three different
locations mentioned. This left me with Joseph Openshaw as the only
suspect. I just needed to confirm this, and the fact that the
murderer was able to use the same method of killing, that is by
placing the victims at the edge of water, pointed again to
Joseph Openshaw as the likely suspect. I also confirmed this
through the police, and I now have enough evidence to arrest him."

"I mean that we shall use their own weapon against them. I have
obtained from the East India Company one of their sailing
registers. It is a large volume, but it is not so difficult to
make out, though it is printed in a very strange character. I
have ascertained the name of the vessel which left Dundee for
London on the 12th of January--the very day that Openshaw
received his last letter. It is the 'Lone Star,' and it is
expected in London to-morrow, or at the latest, on Saturday.
Well, as there are these orange pips, we shall put a few orange
pips in the cabin of the 'Lone Star,' and then the crew may
interpret the sign as they think best. I shall leave for London
in the morning."


"I mean that we shall use their methods against themselves. We
shall make them use their own weapon. It is an even-handed game,
Watson, an even-handed game. What do you think of that?" He
rubbed his hands together, with an expression of the most
intense satisfaction.  "They will find it rather a cold morning
for their little excursion. I have given my orders, and all will
be as it should be. That was rather a clever shot, Watson. Was
it not?"

"Clever?"

"Yes, the whole thing was a clever combination of deduction and
deception. I knew that the man was a seaman--an old sailor--and
that he would not hesitate to make use of a vessel in carrying
out his plot. I had already formed my plan to locate him, and
then it was my intention to place the matter at once in the hands
of the authorities. That would have been my usual procedure. But
this morning's news showed me that it would be unsafe to do so. So
I was forced to resort to other means. It is true that it is a
very daring game, and quite outside the recognised limits of
criminal procedure, but the man was a deadly one, and the stake
was his own life and the life of young Openshaw, so I felt
justified. I think," he added with an air of triumph, "that I
have earned his gratitude."

He held up his hand, and I saw that he had a small packet of
dried orange pips in his palm. "Look here!" said he. "I have
found traces of several recent calls upon some of our friends in
the City. I have also ascertained that this sailing-ship, the 'Lone
Star', which left Port of London three weeks ago and is now well
out in the Atlantic, has James Calhoun on board as a passenger.
He, as it turns out, was the Colonel's closest associate in the
South, and was known to have been concerned in some of those
terrible affairs which brought about the break-up of the Klan.
The other men will soon be traced, but for the moment he is the
most important." He chuckled to himself and rubbed his hands.
"Now then," said he, "we have a few things to do. Firstly, the
police must be told of Calhoun's probable presence on that
ship, and that they may seize him immediately when he lands. This
done, we have a little bit of work to do on our own account. In the
meantime, my dear Watson, let me suggest that our supper be
delayed until we have first had a talk with Mr. Joseph Openshaw
about this singular matter."

"I have them, I tell you," said Holmes, with a confidence which
reassured me.  "I have found their headquarters.  They are
sailing out of London tonight. The 'Lone Star', a three-master
bound for Brazil.  I have seen their faces.  I have their
names. I know their secret."  He paused, his face a mask of grim
determination.  "And I intend to repay them in their own coin."


He took an orange from the cupboard, and tearing it to pieces he
squeezed out the pips upon the table. Of these he took five and
thrust them into an envelope. On the inside of the flap he wrote
"S. H. for J. O." Then he sealed it and addressed it to "Captain
James Calhoun, Barque 'Lone Star,' Savannah, Georgia."

"That will await him when he enters port," said he, chuckling.
"It may give him a sleepless night. He will find it as sure a
precursor of his fate as Openshaw did before him."

"And who is this Captain Calhoun?"

"The leader of the gang. I shall have the others, but he first."

"How did you trace it, then?"

He took a large sheet of paper from his pocket, all covered with
dates and names.

"I then examined the Dundee case, and found that the 'Lone Star'
had been in port there in the end of December, and that she had
cleared for Savannah, Georgia, in the beginning of January. Then
I turned to my files of American newspapers for the last few
years and discovered a series of strange entries which refer to
the murder of two men, one of whom was the celebrated planter,
Elias Openshaw, and another a certain Colonel Gresham, who was
a fellow-soldier of Openshaw's. They were both killed under the
most peculiar circumstances, and the murders were never traced
home. There is a third man involved in this same mystery--one
Joseph Openshaw. Now what connection can there be between all
these events and the death of John Openshaw?"


"I then examined the Dundee case. It was the 'Lone Star' again.
This was enough to give me a strong clue. The ship was a sailing
vessel, and I knew that it would take about seven weeks to make
the voyage from Pondicherry. The dates of the arrival and
departure of the 'Lone Star' were quite consistent with my theory.
Then, of course, I had to look into the East London case. There I
found the same ship again and saw that she had recently returned
to port. I made inquiries at the docks, and learned that she was
expected to sail to-morrow, for Savannah. I have already sent a
telegram to the local police and have secured their assistance
in arresting the captain and his crew when she leaves the
docks."

"But how did you identify them?"

"Oh, that is quite simple. I have the names of three who acted in
the deaths of Openshaw's uncle and father from the information
which was contained in the diary. I have only to compare these
names with the ship's register."

"And you are certain of this Calhoun?"

"I am as certain of Captain James Calhoun as I am of my own
existence. It is a matter of demonstration, Watson, as clear as
A, B, C.

"I then sought for the name of the captain. It was James Calhoun.
I next inquired at the offices of the 'Lone Star's' owners, and
found that she had sailed with a cargo of cotton, which is
always a suspicious circumstance when associated with ships of
Southern origin. I then, by a process of elimination, which I
need not weary you with, narrowed the field down to the only
vessel which had touched at Dundee and had afterwards sailed for
London. That vessel was, of course, the 'Lone Star'."

"But how did you get the other names?"

"From the American papers which contained accounts of the trial of
the Ku Klux Klan. There were some very strange stories of
murder and violence among the planters in Florida, and one of the
chief criminals was a fellow named Joseph Openshaw--a name which
certainly ought to be familiar to us, and was to you, I
remember."

"Elias, the Colonel, and the other one--Joseph!"

"Exactly! They were brothers. They were both in Florida at the
time of the war, but I did not get at their connection until
yesterday afternoon. It seems that Joseph had been the Colonel's
agent, and that the latter had never completely cleared himself
of the suspicions of the Klan in spite of his desertion of them
for the North. When he died Elias's papers must have come to
Joseph, and later still into the hands of John Openshaw. The
Klan must have made investigations into John's life, and
discovered where he was; hence the renewal of their threats in
the form of the three warnings. As for the sundial," continued
Sherlock Holmes, "that is a strange point, but I think we may
assume as a working hypothesis that it was simply a coincidence,
and that it was chosen by the K. K. K. because it stood on the
lawn, and was therefore in a conspicuous place. Now for James
Calhoun."

"I then examined the list of vessels which cleared from London
during those same months, and found that, among others, there was
one, the 'Lone Star,' a three-masted schooner, which was bound
for some port in the Southern States. Her master was James
Calhoun. I then sought for the 'Lone Star' in the Dundee
registers, and discovered that she had arrived there from
Pondicherry on January 3rd, '83, and had sailed again on January
12th. It was, therefore, clear that the vessel which carried the
men who made the first threat had arrived at Dundee."

"Excellent!"

"But there was better to come. It appeared that the vessel had
been chartered in London, and the captain was an American of
violent and lawless disposition. I ascertained his present
whereabouts from the shipping agents. The 'Lone Star' has been
lying at Savannah since last June. This morning I dispatched a
telegram to my agent at Savannah, and he has wired back to me
that he has seen Captain Calhoun and knows that the papers are
on board."

"Then why have you not sent him straight to justice?"

"I then sought out the owners of the 'Lone Star,' and found that
she belonged to a wealthy Southern planter, who, it appeared,
had made a considerable fortune during the war. I obtained a
photograph of this gentleman, and I have no doubt that it is the
same man whom I saw yesterday in the City. I had no difficulty
in tracing him. I found that he had arrived in England about the
time that we might expect from Pondicherry. He had, as I
ascertained from his associates, the same singular tastes and
habits as his compatriots. He lived in seclusion and was
peculiarly averse to society. He kept to himself and was only
seen with the ship's crew. I watched him for two days, and it
appears that he is waiting here until the arrival of his vessel.
I found out from the crew that he is the captain of his own
ship, that he left England on the 10th of March, and that his
vessel is due to arrive from Savannah next week. I have no
doubt, therefore, that he is the same man."

"But what proof have you of his guilt?"

"That must come from what follows. I have the other names from
Openshaw's paper; we have only to find their whereabouts to put
the whole thing together. I think that he is waiting here to
complete the business which has already been so disastrously
commenced."

"I searched the Dundee records, and when I found that the barque
'Lone Star' was there in January, '85, my suspicion became a
certainty. I then inquired as to the vessels which lay at present
in the port of London."

"Yes?"

"Nothing. Captain Calhoun will get my message. He is as good as
in my hands. The others I may have to work for, but he is already
caught. When he is safely in prison, we can talk of hunting the
rest of his gang. With such a clue as those orange pips, one
might find the other members of the society. The police are
useless. They have missed it all. Even you, my dear Watson,
would have missed this, and you are a man of resource. But there
was just one little point which made me certain. In the first
place, he had already failed to kill John Openshaw, and for this
reason the ship would go to Savannah and not to Texas. After that
it was easy to confirm the suspicions by the Lloyd's records."

"Nothing. I have played my game, and it is for them to play
theirs. But I have a notion that the game is nearly over. I shall
go down to Horsham to-morrow and look after young Openshaw's
affairs. I think that our friend the inspector may congratulate
himself upon the accidental death of John Openshaw. If the case
had gone into court, as it certainly would have done, had
Openshaw lived, then it would have been very awkward for certain
people--among others, the chief witness, Joseph Openshaw, alias
James Calhoun. And now, Watson, I think that we may go to bed."
"My dear Watson, we are going to do nothing. The game is played
and the stake is won. That letter will reach its destination, and
the effect will be curious. I want to see how a man behaves who
knows that his past is about to overtake him. I shall take it as
a compliment if, next time we meet, you tell me that the 'Lone
Star' has arrived at Savannah and that its captain has been
arrested. Then I will tell you the true story of the K. K. K.
and of the death of the Openshaws."

"Nothing for the present. I have done all that I can. The
rest must be left to the authorities. I have given them a clue
which they will not be likely to neglect, and it is possible
that before many weeks are past we may hear of Captain James
Calhoun and of his associates being brought to justice."

"Nothing. My work is done. The game is played out. I have
recovered the papers, and I have laid my hand upon the man who
sent those murderous messages. Captain James Calhoun will never
trouble the Openshaws again. The police will have the documents
in the morning; and they may then proceed to the arrest. You
may be sure that when I have spun my web they may take the flies
as they will, but not before."

"Oh, I have my hand upon him. He and the two mates, are as I
learn, the only native-born Americans in the ship. The others are
Finns and Germans. I know, also, that they were all three away
from the ship last night. I had it from the stevedore who has
been loading their cargo. By the time that their sailing-ship
reaches Savannah the mail-boat will have carried this letter, and
the cable will have informed the police of Savannah that these
three gentlemen are badly wanted here upon a charge of murder."
